sections.title: Explain a bond with a shared pair and two nuclei
paragraphs: A single covalent bond is one shared pair of electrons between two bonded atoms. In H₂, each neutral hydrogen atom contributes one electron. There are two distinct electrons in the molecule, even though both atoms count the shared pair towards their first shell.

The negatively charged shared electrons are attracted to both positively charged nuclei. This electrostatic attraction holds the bonded atoms together. The bond is not an attraction between two negative electrons or a transfer that leaves one positive and one negative hydrogen ion.

A double bond has two shared pairs and a triple bond has three. Their shared electron counts are therefore four and six. A displayed line counts a pair, not a single electron. Lone pairs are non-bonding outer electrons; they are not automatically extra covalent bonds.

These examples explain the bond and counting principles. The complete specified molecule-drawing collection is audited separately under 1.46; this explanation does not certify that all required diagrams have been reviewed.

example.question: A sketch puts one dot and one cross between two H symbols. Explain what is shared and what attracts it.
steps: The dot and cross represent one electron from each H atom, making a single shared pair.
That pair is attracted to both positive hydrogen nuclei.
Both atoms count the same two electrons towards their full first shell; the molecule does not contain four distinct electrons.
example.explanation: Identify the particles, arrangement and relevant attraction or mobile charge carrier, then connect that feature to the observed property.

practice.question: A student says that a triple bond contains three electrons and that two electrons attract each other to form a bond. Correct both statements.
practice.answer: A triple bond contains three shared pairs, or six shared electrons. The bonding explanation uses attraction between shared negative electrons and both positive nuclei, not attraction between two negative electrons.
practice.explanation: Name the level of structure involved; a correct observation alone does not supply its explanation.

commonMistakes: Do not interchange bonding within a molecule with attractions between molecules. Charge and mobility are separate properties.

sections.title: Use the right attraction for a molecular change of state
paragraphs: Strong covalent bonds hold atoms inside each simple molecule; intermolecular attractions act between molecules. Ordinary melting or boiling separates or rearranges molecules without generally breaking their internal bonds. A low boiling temperature therefore does not show that the covalent bonds inside the molecules are weak.

An invented comparable molecular series has supplied relative molecular masses 40, 70 and 100 and boiling temperatures −10, 25 and 60 °C. The rising temperature is consistent with generally stronger intermolecular attractions as molecular mass increases in a comparable series. These values are fictional, not an identified chemical dataset.

At 20 °C and the same pressure, the first supplied substance is above its boiling temperature and is gaseous. For the other two, their melting temperatures must also be known to distinguish liquid from solid. A boiling temperature alone cannot prove they are liquids. The table includes melting temperatures to make that comparison possible.

Molecular mass is a general trend, not a universal ordering rule between unrelated substances. Molecular shape and the kind of intermolecular attraction can change an actual comparison. More electrons or larger molecules do not justify claiming that the internal covalent bonds are being broken during boiling.

Ordinary neutral simple molecular substances lack mobile ions or delocalised charge carriers through the substance, so they usually do not conduct electricity. An aqueous molecular compound can react or ionise to provide mobile ions; hydrogen chloride in water illustrates why “every covalent substance and every solution is an insulator” is false.

example.question: Use the fictional table to identify the state of each material at 20 °C and explain the boiling trend.
steps: P has boiling temperature −10 °C, so at 20 °C it is gas under the supplied conditions.
Q has melting temperature −30 °C and boiling temperature 25 °C: 20 °C lies between, so it is liquid.
R has melting temperature 35 °C, so at 20 °C it is solid.

In the supplied comparable series, generally stronger intermolecular attractions require more energy to separate the heavier molecules. This is not a claim that all unrelated molecules follow exactly that order.
example.explanation: Identify the particles, arrangement and relevant attraction or mobile charge carrier, then connect that feature to the observed property.

practice.question: A fourth substance has relative molecular mass 130 and boils at 40 °C. Does that observation contradict every molecular explanation? During boiling, which attractions are overcome? Why might a solution of a covalent acid conduct?
practice.answer: No. A general mass trend does not establish an exact rule for unrelated molecules; shape and attraction type can matter. Ordinary boiling overcomes intermolecular attractions, leaving internal covalent bonds intact. An acid can form mobile ions in water; those ions, rather than the original neutral molecules, carry charge.
practice.explanation: Name the level of structure involved; a correct observation alone does not supply its explanation.

commonMistakes: Do not interchange bonding within a molecule with attractions between molecules. Charge and mobility are separate properties.

sections.title: Compare carbon networks with separate fullerene cages
paragraphs: A giant covalent network extends through many atoms with strong covalent bonds. Disrupting that network requires a large energy input, explaining its very high thermal-change temperatures. Real carbon behaviour depends on pressure and can involve sublimation; do not invent an ordinary melting/boiling measurement from a simple classroom sketch.

Diamond has each carbon bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network. Bonds act throughout the structure, making pure diamond very hard. Its electrons do not provide the mobile pathway needed for ordinary electrical conduction, so pure diamond is an insulator.

Graphite has each carbon bonded to three others in hexagonal sheets. Strong bonds within the layers give high thermal stability, while weaker attractions between layers allow sliding and explain its softness. Delocalised electrons move along the layers and carry charge. “Soft means low melting point” confuses two different structural effects.

C₆₀ consists of separate molecules with 60 carbon atoms in each cage. Strong covalent bonds hold each cage together; comparatively weak attractions join separate cages in the molecular solid. Pure solid C₆₀ is much softer and less thermally resistant than diamond and is a poor conductor compared with graphite. It is not a giant network merely because 60 is a large atom count.

The comparisons refer to the ordinary undoped materials in this teaching model. They do not claim that modified carbon materials, different pressures or every direction in graphite have identical properties. A structural explanation must specify which bonds or charge carriers matter.

example.question: A supplied carbon sample is soft, conducts along sheets, and resists high temperatures. Which listed allotrope best matches it, and how are these properties compatible?
steps: Graphite fits the supplied sheet structure and mobile electrons.
Layers slide because attractions between them are much weaker than the covalent bonds within them.
Strong bonds within layers account for high thermal stability; delocalised electrons along layers account for conduction. No contradiction follows from softness.
example.explanation: Identify the particles, arrangement and relevant attraction or mobile charge carrier, then connect that feature to the observed property.

practice.question: Compare pure diamond and pure solid C₆₀ for hardness, ordinary conduction and the attraction disrupted on a thermal change. Is C₆₀ a covalent compound?
practice.answer: Diamond is very hard and ordinarily insulating; disrupting its giant network needs strong covalent bonds to be broken. C₆₀ is a softer molecular solid and a poor conductor; separation of intact cages mainly overcomes intermolecular attractions. C₆₀ contains only carbon, so it is an allotrope of an element, not a compound.
practice.explanation: Name the level of structure involved; a correct observation alone does not supply its explanation.

commonMistakes: Do not interchange bonding within a molecule with attractions between molecules. Charge and mobility are separate properties.

rows: Each C bonded to 4; giant 3D network
Hard; no ordinary mobile charge pathway
Each C bonded to 3 within sheets
Sheets slide; mobile electrons conduct along sheets
Weaker attractions between cages; soft, poor conductor

sections.title: Keep mobile electrons in a metal when its layers shift (Paper 2C)
paragraphs: A two-dimensional metallic model labels positive metal ions and delocalised electrons between them. The regular ion positions represent a slice through a three-dimensional lattice. The electrons are shared through the structure rather than attached to one ion or one isolated electron pair.

The retained drawing now represents an illustrative monovalent patch with nine positive cores and nine negative electron symbols per panel. Its finite patch and symbol positions are bookkeeping, not actual electron locations. An actual metal is overall neutral; the bond is electrostatic attraction between positive cores and delocalised electrons.

A solid metal can conduct while its ion positions remain fixed because delocalised electrons can move and carry charge. Ion movement through the solid is not required. In ordinary molten metal, mobile electrons remain charge carriers; ordinary ionic melts instead conduct through mobile ions.

Malleability means that a metal can be pressed or hammered into a different shape. When layers slide, positive ions remain surrounded by delocalised electrons and the attraction persists. It is inaccurate to say that all metallic bonding disappears or that ions become neutral as soon as the layer shifts.

Many metals have relatively high melting temperatures because overcoming strong metallic attractions requires substantial energy, but this is a typical property, not an exception-free classification test. The source requires metallic drawing, bonding and property explanations for Paper 2C only.

example.question: A drawing shows regular positive circles, e⁻ symbols between them and a second panel with one row shifted. Explain what each represents and why the metal can bend and still conduct.
steps: The circles represent positive metal ions; e⁻ symbols represent delocalised electrons, not negative ions.
When a layer shifts, attraction between the positive cores and electrons continues, allowing deformation.
Mobile delocalised electrons carry current through the solid; the positive ions do not have to travel through it.
example.explanation: Identify the particles, arrangement and relevant attraction or mobile charge carrier, then connect that feature to the observed property.

practice.question: Correct a model that labels the circles as neutral atoms, places no mobile electrons between them, and says a solid metal conducts only because the circles flow. Which particle carries charge in molten sodium chloride instead?
practice.answer: Label the lattice particles positive metal ions and include delocalised electrons throughout the model. Electron mobility allows solid-metal conduction; the positive ions do not flow through its solid lattice. Molten sodium chloride conducts through mobile Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. The substances use different charge carriers.
practice.explanation: Name the level of structure involved; a correct observation alone does not supply its explanation.

commonMistakes: Do not interchange bonding within a molecule with attractions between molecules. Charge and mobility are separate properties.

diagram.alt: Two original monovalent metallic patch models each show nine positive ion symbols and nine electron labels, with one middle row shifted in the second panel.
diagram.caption: A two-dimensional model for Paper 2C. Symbol positions are illustrative; positive ions remain attracted to delocalised electrons when a layer shifts.

sections.title: Count single, double and triple shared pairs
paragraphs: H₂ has two outer electrons, forming one shared pair and no lone pairs. Each H counts those same two electrons towards a full first shell. There are only two distinct electrons in the whole molecule.

O₂ has twelve outer electrons. Its double bond uses four electrons in two shared pairs; each O retains four non-bonding electrons as two lone pairs. Each atom counts four shared plus four non-bonding electrons locally, while the molecule total remains twelve.
N₂ has ten outer electrons. Three shared pairs use six electrons and each N retains one lone pair, supplying the other four. Each N counts six shared plus two non-bonding electrons for an octet.
Use the panel key: dots belong to the left atom and crosses to the right. A shared pair contains one from each. These planar layouts do not establish the location or orbit of an individual electron.

example.question: Check an N₂ drawing with a triple bond and one lone pair on each nitrogen. How many distinct outer electrons are present?
steps: Three shared pairs contribute six electrons.
The two lone pairs contribute four more, giving ten distinct electrons.
Each N locally counts six shared electrons and its own two lone-pair electrons, giving eight.
example.explanation: Count each distinct electron once, then count each shared pair around both bonded atoms. Check the formula, bond order and lone pairs.

practice.question: An O₂ drawing has a double bond and three lone pairs on each oxygen. Is it valid? Compare its total with H₂.
practice.answer: No. Four bonding electrons plus twelve non-bonding electrons makes sixteen, but two O atoms supply only twelve. O₂ needs two lone pairs on each O, not three. H₂ supplies two electrons and uses them in one shared pair with no lone pairs.
practice.explanation: Oxygen supplies twelve outer electrons. The proposed drawing adds four electrons that neither atom supplies.

commonMistakes: Shared electrons count for both shells but only once in the molecule total; a displayed bond line is a pair, not one electron.

diagram.alt: Original diatomic covalent models with each molecule named and a dot/cross source key; shared and lone pairs are shown.
diagram.caption: Original outer-electron diagrams. The layouts are bookkeeping, not measured molecular shapes. Read the source key separately for each panel.

sections.title: Distinguish a halogen pair from a hydrogen halide
paragraphs: A halogen atom supplies seven outer electrons in this model. Cl₂ therefore has fourteen, arranged as one shared pair between the atoms and three lone pairs on each chlorine. The chlorine on either side counts eight electrons locally.

HCl supplies eight outer electrons: one from H and seven from Cl. Its single shared pair counts towards H’s full first shell and Cl’s octet. Only Cl has three lone pairs; adding lone pairs to hydrogen invents electrons.

The same outer-count method applies to the other neutral diatomic halogens and hydrogen halides specified by these groups. Change the element symbol and check the formula before copying a pattern. The diagram is covalent sharing; it is not a picture of the ions present after an acid reacts with water.

example.question: Check the HCl panel and compare its distinct electron count with Cl₂.
steps: HCl uses one shared pair plus three Cl lone pairs: 2 + 6 = 8 outer electrons.
Cl₂ uses one shared pair plus six lone pairs: 2 + 12 = 14.
H has a two-electron shell; each Cl has an octet. A full molecule count must not count a shared pair twice.

practice.question: Using the same model, describe the outer-electron diagram for Br₂ and for HF. Where are the lone pairs?
practice.answer: Br₂ has a single shared pair and three lone pairs on each Br, fourteen distinct outer electrons. HF has one shared pair, three lone pairs on F and none on H, eight distinct outer electrons. Dots and crosses distinguish the original atom sources in each drawing.
practice.explanation: The group-7 atom has seven outer electrons, so one shared pair and three lone pairs supply its octet; hydrogen needs only a pair.

commonMistakes: Shared electrons count for both shells but only once in the molecule total; a displayed bond line is a pair, not one electron.

sections.title: Check water, ammonia and carbon dioxide locally and globally
paragraphs: H₂O supplies eight outer electrons: six from O and one from each H. There are two O–H single bonds and two O lone pairs. NH₃ also supplies eight: five from N plus three from H, making three single bonds and one N lone pair.

CO₂ supplies sixteen: four from C and six from each O. Draw O=C=O with two shared pairs per double bond. Each O also has two lone pairs, while C has none in this model. The eight bonding electrons plus eight lone-pair electrons account for all sixteen.

The source key differs between panels, so read it before identifying contributions. An identical mark can be used for more than one atom; the pair’s position identifies the bond. Each of these models gives H a two-electron shell and the other atoms an octet.
Do not infer that water is linear or ammonia is flat from these page layouts. They are electron-accounting diagrams, not measurements of three-dimensional molecular shape.

example.question: Compare the non-bonding electrons in water and ammonia even though both have eight outer electrons in total.
steps: Water uses four electrons in two shared pairs, leaving four as two O lone pairs.
Ammonia uses six in three shared pairs, leaving two as one N lone pair.
Both totals are eight, but their bond/lone-pair arrangements differ.

practice.question: A CO₂ sketch has two single C–O bonds and three lone pairs on each O, with no other electrons. Does its total of sixteen make it correct?
practice.answer: No. The total may be sixteen, but C counts only four surrounding shared electrons rather than an octet. The course model uses two double bonds and two lone pairs on each O. Global totals and each atom’s local shell must both be checked.
practice.explanation: The single-bond drawing has the correct global total but leaves carbon with only four surrounding electrons. Both checks are necessary.

sections.title: Check each carbon when two carbons share electrons
paragraphs: Methane has four C–H single bonds, using eight outer electrons. Ethane has six C–H single bonds and one C–C single bond: seven pairs, fourteen outer electrons. Ethene has four C–H single bonds and a C=C double bond: six pairs, twelve outer electrons.

Count a double bond as two shared pairs. In ethene, each carbon counts two hydrogen bonds plus the two pairs in the carbon–carbon double bond, giving an octet. In ethane, each carbon has three hydrogen bonds and one carbon bond.

In the two-carbon panels, the left carbon uses dots and the right uses crosses. Each H uses the opposite mark to the carbon it bonds to. Several atoms can use the same mark: it is a bookkeeping convention, not a claim that all dots come from one element.

There are no carbon lone pairs in these neutral models. Check the number of H symbols against the molecular formula before assigning electrons; a correct-looking carbon octet cannot repair an extra hydrogen atom.

example.question: Show why ethane has fourteen distinct shared electrons but each carbon locally counts eight.
steps: Six C–H bonds plus one C–C bond gives seven shared pairs, or fourteen electrons.
Each C participates in four single bonds and locally counts eight shared electrons.
The C–C pair is included for each carbon’s local count but only once in the whole-molecule count.

practice.question: A sketch labelled C₂H₄ has a single C–C bond and only four C–H bonds, with no lone pairs or charges. Is it the valid ethene model? Compare the total for CH₄.
practice.answer: No. That sketch has only five shared pairs (ten electrons) and each C participates in only three single bonds. Ethene needs a C=C double bond: six pairs/twelve electrons. Methane has four single bonds/eight shared electrons.
practice.explanation: Replacing a double bond by a single pair removes two electrons from the molecule and two from each carbon’s local shell count.

sections.title: Keep halogen lone pairs when a hydrogen is replaced
paragraphs: Replacing one hydrogen by chlorine preserves one single bond to carbon but changes the available outer-electron total. CH₃Cl supplies 4 + 3 + 7 = 14: four single bonds use eight and the chlorine’s three lone pairs use six.

C₂H₅Cl supplies 8 + 5 + 7 = 20. Its C–C bond, five C–H bonds and one C–Cl bond make seven shared pairs (fourteen electrons); the chlorine’s three lone pairs add six. Each carbon counts four bond pairs, and chlorine counts one shared pair plus three lone pairs.

Read the local key in the two-carbon panel. Each hydrogen or chlorine uses the opposite mark to its bonded carbon; its lone-pair marks retain that same original-atom source. The marks do not distinguish different physical kinds of electron.

For another neutral halogen substitution up to two carbons, retain four bonds around each carbon, one bond around each H or halogen, and three lone pairs on a single-bonded halogen. Recheck the formula and total rather than adding a halogen without removing the replaced hydrogen.

example.question: Explain why chloroethane has twenty outer electrons although ethane has fourteen.
steps: Both drawings have seven shared pairs, using fourteen electrons.
The Cl atom contributes six additional non-bonding electrons in its three lone pairs.
Total 20 also agrees with two C atoms (8), five H (5) and Cl (7). Replacing H’s one electron by Cl’s seven adds six.

practice.question: Describe a CH₂Cl₂ outer-electron model and count its distinct outer electrons. A learner leaves out both chlorine lone-pair sets: what is missing?
practice.answer: Carbon has two C–H and two C–Cl single bonds, giving four pairs/eight bonding electrons. Each Cl needs three lone pairs, adding twelve non-bonding electrons. Total4+2+14=20. Omitting both sets loses twelve electrons and gives each chlorine an incomplete local shell.
practice.explanation: Halogen lone pairs do not form extra bonds to carbon, but they must appear in a full outer-electron diagram.
